hero.subtitle: The 93% that wasn't.
hero.lead: My query router reported 93.3% accuracy. I found out why that number was wrong, measured the real one, and rebuilt the model until the honest score was worth shipping.

product.title: A small model that decides who answers
product.body: Not every question needs an expensive AI. RouteJudge reads each question, labels how hard it is, and sends it to the cheapest model that can answer it well. The label is the whole product: get it wrong in one direction and users get bad answers; in the other, you pay for nothing.
product.classifierNote: reads the question, never answers it

number.caption: The accuracy my classifier reported. It looked finished.

investigation.title: Four clues it wasn't
investigation.intro: Before tuning anything, I audited the whole pipeline: data, labels, training runs and the live app. Each clue had evidence behind it.

clues.title: The exam had the answers
clues.body: Every validation question was a reworded copy of a training question: "Please What is a vector?" next to "What is a vector?". A lookup table with no model at all scored the same 93.3%.

clues.title: It learned topics, not difficulty
clues.body: The labels followed the subject: math was 99% EASY, creative writing 100% HARD. Guessing from the topic alone scored {{shortcut}}%. So "integrate x²eˣ by parts" went to the cheapest model.

clues.title: It never trained on the new data
clues.body: The run took 834 training steps where the new dataset needed 1,674. The cloud volume still held the old {{stale}}-row files, not the {{local}} rows everyone assumed.

clues.title: Production asked a different question
clues.body: The live app wrapped every query in tags and instructions the model never saw in training, so even the real model was answering a different prompt.

honest.title: Then I measured it properly
honest.body: I built a frozen test set of {{items}} questions in English, Portuguese and Chinese, none of them seen in training and every label checked against a written rubric. The same model scored barely above always answering MEDIUM.
honest.statCheap: Sent to too cheap a model
honest.matrixTitle: Where the old model went wrong
honest.matrixCaption: Rows are the true difficulty, columns the model's answer. Most hard questions landed in EASY or MEDIUM.

steps.title: One definition
steps.body: Difficulty is how much reasoning a good answer needs. Topic, language, length and politeness don't count.

steps.title: Real questions
steps.body: {{train}} training questions, {{wildchat}} of them from real users, in English, Portuguese and Chinese. None written by me, so the model can't learn my style.

steps.title: An open teacher with a gate
steps.body: An open-source model (Mistral Small 24B) labeled the data, only after agreeing {{agreement}}% with the human-checked test labels.

steps.title: Shortcuts removed
steps.body: Topic alone now predicts the label {{now}}% of the time, down from {{before}}%.

steps.title: A reality check
steps.body: Can a cheap model really answer what I call EASY? The local model solved {{localEasy}}% of EASY questions and only {{localHard}}% of HARD ones. The old EASY tier solved just {{tinyEasy}}%, so I moved it.

training.title: Two models, one honest bug
training.body: Same data, same settings, two base models: TinyLlama 1.1B and Qwen3 1.7B, fine-tuned on Modal. Checkpoints were picked on a separate validation set, never on the test set.
training.chartSubtitle: Macro-F1 on {{valid}} validation questions, measured every 100 steps
training.bugBody: Served locally, TinyLlama started answering "EASELY". The trained adapter was fine; the merge step inside the training job wasn't. Merging again from the saved adapter fixed it, verified on 60 questions before anything shipped.

results.title: {{value}}%, measured the same way as the {{old}}%
results.body: Both new models were scored on the same frozen test set, through the real backend, exactly as users reach them.

targets.languageNote: EN {{en}}% · PT {{pt}}% · ZH {{zh}}% on the same tasks

results.zeroErrors: Across {{items}} test questions, Qwen3 never confused EASY with HARD. Every remaining mistake is between neighbors.

shipping.title: From experiment to product
items: The live app now classifies with Qwen3 v3: {{value}}% instead of {{old}}%.
Confidence is the model's own probability for its label. It used to be a constant 0.85 for every query.
The parser takes the label the model actually said first, instead of always preferring EASY.
A "tier floor" lets history upgrade a route but never downgrade it to a weaker model.
The whole retune used about ${{cost}} of cloud GPU time.

dashboard.alt: RouteJudge dashboard. A question was classified as Hard, 99% sure, and routed to GPT-4. The result card shows an estimated cost of $0.03, a router time of 0.37 seconds, and a typical answer time marked Not measured.
dashboard.caption: The result card. The router's own time is measured on every request; when a model's answer time was never measured, the card says so instead of guessing.

stats.alt: RouteJudge statistics page with four stat cards (48 queries, 0.41 s average router time, $1.12 saved, satisfaction rate empty), a donut chart of queries by difficulty (Easy 18, Medium 21, Hard 9), and a cost-savings card showing 78% saved compared to GPT-4.
stats.caption: Statistics. Satisfaction stays empty on purpose: with ratings that were always five stars, any number there would be the 93% all over again.

history.alt: RouteJudge history page with a detail dialog open for query 47: a Hard question about infinitely many primes, routed to GPT-4, cost $0.03, latency 0.37 seconds, not rated.
history.caption: History, with one query opened: every routing decision is logged with its model, cost and time.
